name: Merlot

lines.s10: Merlot is the soft red of Bordeaux's Right Bank: ripe plum, black cherry and a little chocolate, with a smooth, round feel.
lines.s20: Merlot is the grape behind Pomerol and Saint-Émilion, and it ripens earlier and drinks softer than Cabernet Sauvignon. Expect black plum and black cherry with a touch of cocoa, on a round, fleshy body that is easy to like from the first glass.
lines.s45: Merlot puts the soft heart into red Bordeaux, and on the Right Bank, in Pomerol and Saint-Émilion, it leads the blend. It tastes of ripe plum and black cherry, with a note of chocolate, and it feels round and smooth, with gentle tannin. A year or more in oak barrels adds cedar and vanilla. Bordeaux tends to be firmer and more savoury, while California is typically plusher and riper. Put it beside roast duck, mushrooms or a slow braise. The French blackbird, the merle, is as dark as the grape and said to be fond of it, and may well have given Merlot its name.
lines.sale: Merlot gives you the depth of a serious red without the hard edges: plum, black cherry and a smooth finish. It is the bottle for a table sharing duck, pork and mushrooms, where a firmer wine would get in the way.

glass.lead: Black plum and black cherry with cocoa and a touch of bay leaf, on a round, fleshy body with soft tannin.

ladder.where: Pomerol and Saint-Émilion, Hawke's Bay, the north east of Italy
Napa Valley, Sonoma and Chile's Central Valley

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity medium, tannin medium and soft, alcohol medium plus to high, body medium plus to full.

old.where: Bordeaux's Right Bank, Pomerol and Saint-Émilion; north east Italy
old.glass: Right Bank wines tend to be savoury and structured: black plum and red cherry with truffle, forest floor and cedar, fresh acidity, fine tannin and alcohol short of high. North east Italy's are usually lighter and softer.
old.cellar: Right Bank wines are mostly blends, with Cabernet Franc and often a little Cabernet Sauvignon, aged in French oak barrels, a share of them new.

new.where: California, Washington State, Chile, Hawke's Bay and Stellenbosch
new.glass: Typically plusher and riper: black cherry, black plum and blackberry jam wrapped in mocha and vanilla, with softer acidity, rounder tannin, a fuller body and higher alcohol.
new.cellar: Usually bottled under the grape's own name, alone or with a little Cabernet; picked riper and often aged in a larger share of new oak.

contrast.why: Bordeaux's mild maritime climate and its cold clay ripen Merlot steadily and keep its freshness and savour. Sunnier New World valleys give more sugar and softer acidity. Bordeaux labels the place, the New World the grape.
contrast.blur: Washington State and Hawke's Bay make firm, fresh Merlot that can pass for Bordeaux, while Tuscany's coast and warm recent vintages on the Right Bank give riper, fuller wines.
contrast.call: Truffle, cedar and fresh acidity with alcohol short of high lean Right Bank; jammy black plum, mocha and vanilla at higher alcohol lean New World.

service.temp: 59 to 63 degrees Fahrenheit, 15 to 17 degrees Celsius: enough warmth to open the aroma.
service.glass: A Bordeaux glass, tall enough to gather the fruit.
service.decant: Taste first: a firm young Right Bank wine can open with air; an old one comes off its sediment.
service.age: Most are ready within five years; Pomerol and Saint-Émilion from good sites keep five to fifteen, a few far longer.

with.why: plum fruit and soft tannin suit the rich meat

with.dish: Mushroom risotto, or anything with truffle
with.why: truffle and forest floor in the wine echo the plate
round fruit and gentle tannin, nothing to fight
ripe fruit and soft tannin sit easily with the dark roux

labels.means: Right Bank Bordeaux place names: the label names the village, and Merlot usually leads the blend.
An appellation with stricter rules, not a classed estate; Grand Cru Classé is the classification above it.
Federal law asks for at least 75 per cent of the named grape; the rest may be Cabernet or another.

guest.a: No, both are dry. Merlot has softer tannin and riper, plummier fruit, so it feels rounder and can seem sweeter, but there is no sugar left in it.

guest.q: What is the difference between the Left Bank and the Right Bank?
guest.a: On the Left Bank, in the Médoc, Cabernet Sauvignon leads and the wines are firmer. On the Right Bank, in Pomerol and Saint-Émilion, Merlot leads and they are rounder and ready sooner.

guest.q: I was told not to order Merlot. Is that fair?
guest.a: It fell out of fashion, not out of quality. Pomerol and Saint-Émilion are built on Merlot, and a well made one has depth as well as softness.

compare.tell: Cabernet Sauvignon shows cassis and firm, drying tannin; Merlot is softer and fleshier, with plum in place of the cassis.
Malbec is darker, with a magenta rim, violet and blueberry; Merlot is ruby and plummy, with none of that violet lift.
Cabernet Franc, a parent of Merlot, is leaner and brighter: raspberry, pencil shavings and green bell pepper where Merlot is rounder, softer and fleshier.

cards.front: Merlot: where is it at home, and who are its parents?
cards.back: Bordeaux's Right Bank: Pomerol on clay, Saint-Émilion on limestone and clay. A study published in 2009 named its parents: Cabernet Franc and the almost lost Magdeleine Noire des Charentes.

cards.front: Merlot blind: Right Bank Bordeaux or the New World, what tips it?
cards.back: Truffle, cedar, fresh acidity and alcohol short of high lean Right Bank. Jammy black plum, mocha, vanilla and higher alcohol lean California or Chile.

cards.front: How does Merlot differ from Cabernet Sauvignon, in the vineyard and the glass?
cards.back: It ripens earlier and suits cold clay. In the glass it is plum where Cabernet is cassis, with softer tannin, a fleshier middle and less cedar.

questions.q: A blind red is deep ruby, with jammy black plum and black cherry, mocha and vanilla, soft acidity, round tannin and high alcohol. The table agrees it is Merlot. Which origin fits it?
questions.exp: Jammy fruit, mocha and vanilla from new oak, soft acidity and high alcohol point to a warm New World site. Pomerol and Saint-Émilion tend to show fresher acidity, truffle and cedar at lower alcohol.

questions.q: A guest enjoys the cedar of a Left Bank Bordeaux but finds it too firm, and asks for a red Bordeaux that is rounder and ready sooner. Which do you bring?
questions.exp: Pomerol is on the Right Bank, where Merlot leads the blend and gives rounder, softer wines. Pauillac, Saint-Estèphe and Saint-Julien are Left Bank villages led by Cabernet Sauvignon.

questions.q: A guest asks how Merlot is related to Cabernet Sauvignon. What do you tell her?
opts: They share a parent, Cabernet Franc
Merlot is a parent of Cabernet Sauvignon
Cabernet Sauvignon is a parent of Merlot
They are unrelated grapes grown side by side
questions.exp: Cabernet Franc is a parent of both. With Sauvignon Blanc it gave Cabernet Sauvignon, and with Magdeleine Noire des Charentes it gave Merlot, so neither is the other's parent.

report: Mode contrast, as the plan fixes it and as TASTE.world, both, requires. The Codex's records on Merlot read true and nothing here departs from them; say is the Court's own respelling.
The ladder has two rungs, moderate and warm, as the Court's grid reads Pomerol and Saint-Émilion moderate and Napa and Sonoma warm; the grape has no true cool home.
The name from merle, the blackbird, is hedged in the spoken line as thought to be: the sources read give two reasons, the colour of the berry and the bird's liking for it, and call neither settled.

The parentage stands on the paper of 2009 in the Australian Journal of Grape and Wine Research, read through its record in the open archive of the French national research institute, and on Wine Grapes. No researcher is named.

Washington as the firmer exception stands on the Codex's own profile. A line the state's wine body is said to publish on mint and cigar box could not be found, so no source of Washington's is cited; mint stands among the notes on a general description of the grape.
The guest question on Merlot's fall from fashion names no film; the Codex's California record dates the film Sideways to 2004.
Chicken and smoked sausage gumbo is the one dish from the Creole table: a soft, ripe red is the usual red with a dark roux.
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open bordeaux.com or hal.inrae.fr directly.

checked.verdict: Sound after ten fixes over two rounds. The parentage of 2009, the blackbird, the federal rule of 75 per cent and the Saint-Émilion ladder were confirmed; the Old World side described one of its three places, named another its own blur excepts and gave the Right Bank a firm tannin the grid reads as round, and three tells parted Merlot from its neighbours by notes both carry.
changed: worlds.contrast.old.glass: The Old World where names north east Italy, but the glass described the Right Bank alone; the lighter, softer Merlot of Friuli and the Veneto is the Codex's own line for the moderate rung.

worlds.contrast.old.cellar: Nearly every wine is a blend, with Cabernet Franc and often a little Cabernet Sauvignon now reads Right Bank wines are mostly blends, with Cabernet Franc and often a little Cabernet Sauvignon. Nearly every wine is a blend is true of the Right Bank and not of north east Italy, which bottles Merlot alone; mostly also leaves room for the near single grape wines of Pomerol.

worlds.contrast.blur: The blur named no warm Old World exception. The Tuscan coast is the Codex's own warm Merlot (Bolgheri in the profile's regions), and its ripe, full wines are the exception a blind taster meets.
glass.ladder, the moderate rung: Truffle is a note of age and earth, not of a moderate climate; red cherry is the Court's own red fruit for Pomerol and Saint-Émilion.

compare, the Malbec tell: Merlot is ruby, with plum and cocoa and none of that violet lift now reads Merlot is ruby and plummy, with none of that violet lift. The tell gave cocoa to Merlot, but the Malbec entry and the Malbec profile list cocoa among Malbec's own notes, so it parted nothing.

worlds.contrast.old.where: Bolgheri stood among the places of the Old World style while the glass described none of its ripe coastal Merlot and the blur, rightly, names the Tuscan coast as the warm exception. It leaves the where and stays in the blur.

worlds.contrast.old.glass: fresh acidity, fine, firm tannin and alcohol short of high now reads fresh acidity, fine tannin and alcohol short of high. Firm tannin for the Right Bank: the grid reads its tannin as round and the reviewed profile as soft, so fine is enough.
worlds.contrast.new.glass: The New World glass and the blur both named Washington as the firm exception; the blur keeps it, beside Hawke's Bay, and the glass is left to describe the typical bottle.

compare, the Cabernet Sauvignon tell: The tell gave cedar to Cabernet alone, but this entry lists cedar among Merlot's own oak notes, and it gave Merlot black cherry, which the Cabernet Sauvignon pilot lists among its own. Cassis, which Merlot does not carry, and the grip now part them, as the reviewed confuse line has it.

compare, the Cabernet Franc tell: Merlot was called plummy against Cabernet Franc, but the Cabernet Franc entry lists red and black plum among its own notes; the round, soft flesh parts them, with the pencil shavings and green pepper Merlot lacks.
open: Mint among the herbal notes stands on general descriptions of the grape, not on a regional body, as the author reported.
North east Italy on the moderate rung stands on the Codex's own regional records; the Court's grid reads no Italian Merlot.
